label: throwawayFrattini
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\langle X\rangle$ is a proper subgroup of $G$, then there exists a maximal subgroup $M$ of $G$ with $\langle X\rangle \leqslant M$.
Of course, $\Phi(G) \leqslant M$.
Hence, $G = \langle \Phi(G), X\rangle \leqslant M < G$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: normal,containedinafrattini
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If  $K\not\leqslant \Phi(G)$, then $K \not\leqslant M$ for some maximal subgroup $M$ of $G$.
By the maximality of $M$ and the normality of $K$, we deduce that $G = KM$.
By Dedekind's Rule and Lemma \ref{throwawayFrattini}, \[H = H \cap KM = K(H \cap M) =\Phi(H)(H \cap M) = (H \cap M) \leqslant M.\]
Now, $K \leqslant H \leqslant M$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: nilpotentimpliesfrattinirespectscontainment
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{nilpotentimpliesfrattinirespectscontainment}
Let $G$ be a nilpotent group.
If $J \leqslant R \leqslant G$, then $\Phi(J) \leqslant \Phi(R)$.
In other words, in nilpotent groups, taking Frattini subgroups respects containments.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $\Phi(J) \not\leqslant \Phi(R)$.
Then, there exists a maximal subgroup $S$ of $R$ with $\Phi(J) \not\leqslant S$.
Because $R$ is nilpotent, we know that $S$ is normal in $R$.
We deduce that $R = \Phi(J)S$.
By Dedekind's Rule and Lemma \ref{throwawayFrattini}, \[ J = J\cap R = J \cap  \Phi(J)S= \Phi(J) (J \cap S) = (J \cap S) \leqslant S.\]
Now, $\Phi(J)\leqslant J\leqslant S$, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: G'intersecthypercenterinfrattini
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{G'intersecthypercenterinfrattini}
If $G$ is any group, then \[ G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_\infty(G) \leqslant \Phi(G).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $J = \Phi(G)$ and, for each non-negative integer $i$, let $D_i = G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_i(G)$.
We shall prove that $D_i \leqslant J$ by induction on $i$.
If $i = 0$, then $D_i = G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_0(G)  = 1 \leqslant J$.

Assume inductively that $D_i \leqslant J$.
Let $M$ be a maximal subgroup of $G$.
If $\mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G) \leqslant M$, then clearly $D_{i+1} \leqslant M$.
Assume that $\mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G) \not\leqslant M$.
Then the normality of $\mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G)$ and the maximality of $M$ imply that $G = \mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G) M$.
Clearly $M \leqslant \mathbf{N}_G(M)$.
Note that $[M, \mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G)] \leqslant [G, \mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G)] \leqslant \mathbf{Z}_i(G)$.
Hence, \[[M, \mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G)] \leqslant G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_i(G) = D_i \leqslant J \leqslant M.\]
So, $\mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G) \leqslant \mathbf{N}_G(M)$.
Now, as $G = \mathbf{Z}_{i+1}(G) M$, we have that $M$ is normal in $G$.
By the maximality of $M$ in $G$, the factor group $G/M$ has precisely two subgroups, and so $G/M$ has prime order.
In particular, $G/M$ is abelian, and $D_{i+1} \leqslant G' \leqslant M$.
In all cases, $D_{i+1} \leqslant M$.
Since $M$ was an  arbitrary maximal subgroup of $G$, we deduce that $D_{i+1} \leqslant J$.
The induction argument goes through.
We conclude that $G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_\infty(G) \leqslant J$, as required.

label: intersections
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{intersections}
Let $G$ be a group and assume that $G  = J \times R$ for subgroups $J$ and $R$ of $G$.
Let $J_1, \ldots, J_n \leqslant J$ and let $R_1,\ldots, R_n \leqslant R$.
Then, \[ \bigcap_{i=1}^n J_iR_i  = \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n J_i\right)\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n R_i\right).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use induction on $n$.
The lemma is trivially true for $n = 1$.
Assume inductively the result for $n$.
Then, given subgroups $J_1, \ldots, J_n, J_{n+1} \leqslant J$ and $R_1, \ldots, R_n, R_{n+1} \leqslant R$, we have by our induction hypothesis that \[ \bigcap_{i=1}^{n+1} J_iR_i = \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n J_iR_i\right) \cap J_{n+1} R_{n+1} = \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n J_i\right)\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n R_i\right)  \cap J_{n+1}R_{n+1}.\]
The containment \[  \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n+1} J_i\right)\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n+1} R_i\right) \leqslant   \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n J_i\right)\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n R_i\right)  \cap J_{n+1}R_{n+1}\] is clear.
Let $g \in   \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n J_i\right)\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n R_i\right)  \cap J_{n+1}R_{n+1}$.
Now, $g = j_0 r_0 = j_1 r_1$ for $j_0 \in \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n J_i\right)$, $r_0 \in  \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^n R_i\right)$, $j_1 \in J_{n+1}$, and $r_1 \in R_{n+1}$.
Hence, $j_1^{-1}j_0 = r_1 r_0^{-1} \in J \cap R = 1$.
So, $j_0 = j_1 \in  \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n+1} J_i\right)$ and $r_0= r_1 \in \left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{n+1} R_i\right) $.
Indeed, the reverse containment holds too.
head: environment

label: coresofcertaintypesofsubgroupsindirectproducts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{coresofcertaintypesofsubgroupsindirectproducts}
Let $G$ be a group and assume that $G = J \times R$ for subgroups $J$ and $R$ of $G$.
Let $V \leqslant J$ and let $W \leqslant R$.
Then \[ (VW)_G = V_J W_R.\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, note that $[V,W] \leqslant [J,R] =1$, and so the product set $VW$ indeed forms a subgroup of $G$.
We compute that
\begin{align*}
(VW)_G = \bigcap_{g \in G} (VW)^g 
            = \bigcap_{\substack{j\in J \\ r\in R}} (VW)^{jr} 
             &= \bigcap_{\substack{j\in J \\ r\in R}} V^{jr} W^{jr} \\
             &=\bigcap_{\substack{j\in J \\ r\in R}} V^j W^r \\
            &\overset{(*)}{=}\left( \bigcap_{j \in J} V^j\right)\left( \bigcap_{r \in R} W^r\right)\\
            &= V_J W_R,
\end{align*}
where $(*)$ holds by Lemma \ref{intersections}.

label: Rose'stheorem
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Rose'stheorem}
Let $G$ be a group and let $p$ be a prime.
Let $J$ be a Frattini normal subgroup of $G$ and assume that $J$ is a $p$-group.
Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
If $J \leqslant \mathbf{Z}(S)$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
head: environment
name: Rose's Theorem

title: Lemma
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group and let $p$ be a prime.
If $P$ and $S$ are Sylow $p$-subgroups of $G$, then $\Phi(P)_G = \Phi(S)_G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Because $\Phi(P)_G$ is a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$, we know that $\Phi(P)_G \leqslant S$.
Assume that $\Phi(P)_G \not\leqslant \Phi(S)$.
Then, there exists a maximal subgroup $R$ of $S$ with $\Phi(P)_G \not\leqslant R$.
Hence, $S = \Phi(P)_GR$.
By Sylow's Theorem, $P = S^g$ for some $g \in G$.
Now, $P = S^g = (\Phi(P)_G R)^g = \Phi(P)_G R^g = \Phi(P) R^g = R^g$ by Lemma \ref{throwawayFrattini}.
So, $|P| = |R^g| = |R| < |S|$, a contradiction.
We deduce that $\Phi(P)_G \leqslant \Phi(S)$ and, since $\Phi(P)_G$ is normal in $G$, we actually have that $\Phi(P)_G \leqslant \Phi(S)_G$.
Reverse the roles of $P$ and $S$ in this argument to see that the reverse containment holds as well.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group.
If $J$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ with $J \leqslant \Psi(G)$, then $J$ is a stictly Frattini subgroup of $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $X$ be an arbitrary subgroup of $G$.
Let $\pi_1 = \pi(G:X)$ and let $\pi_2 = \pi(G: JX)$.
We need to prove that $\pi_1 = \pi_2$.
Since $|G : JX|$ divides $|G : X|$, the containment $\pi_2 \subseteq \pi_1$ certainly holds.

Suppose that $\pi_1 \not\subseteq \pi_2$ and choose $p \in \pi_1 \setminus \pi_2$.
Let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $J$.
Because $J$ is contained in $\Psi(G)$, we know that $J$ is nilpotent.
Hence, $P$ is a characteristic subgroup of $J$.
So, as $J$ is a normal in $G$, we deduce that $P$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
Now, let $Y$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $X$.
Note that $PY$ is a subgroup of $G$, as $P$ is normal in $G$.
In fact, notice that $PY$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $JX$.
Since $p \not\in \pi_2$, we deduce that $PY$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.

Now, as $PY$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$, we know that $\Phi(PY)_G$ is the unique Sylow $p$-subgroup of $\Psi(G)$.
As $P \leqslant J \leqslant \Psi(G)$, we deduce that $P \leqslant \Phi(PY)_G \leqslant \Phi(PY)$ by Sylow's Theorem.
Hence, $PY = \Phi(PY)Y = Y$ by Lemma \ref{throwawayFrattini}.
So $X$ contains a full Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$, contrary to the fact that $p \in \pi_1$.
Hence, $\pi_1 \subseteq \pi_2$.
Combining our containments, we conlude that $\pi_1 = \pi_2$, as wanted.
head: environment

label: G'intersecthypercenter
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{G'intersecthypercenter}
If $G$ is any group, then \[ G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_{\infty}(G) \leqslant \Psi(G).\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $J = \Psi(G)$ and let $Z_i  =  \mathbf{Z}_i(G)$ for each non-negative integer $i$.
Let $D_i = G' \cap Z_i$ for each non-negative integer $i$.
We shall show that $D_i \leqslant J$ by induction on $i$.
If $i = 0$, then $D_i = 1 \leqslant  J$.

Assume inductively that $D_i \leqslant J$.
Let $p$ be a prime and let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $D_{i+1}$.
Because $D_{i+1} \leqslant Z_{i+1}$, we know that $D_{i+1}$ is nilpotent.
Hence, $P$ is a characteristic subgroup of $D_{i+1}$.
Since $D_{i+1}$ is normal in $G$, we deduce that $P$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
Note that $D_{i+1} \leqslant \Phi(G)$ by Lemma \ref{G'intersecthypercenterinfrattini}, and so $P \leqslant \Phi(G)$.
In particular, $P$ is a Frattini normal subgroup of $G$.

Let $R = [G,P]$.
Note that $R \leqslant Z_i$ as $P \leqslant Z_{i+1}$.
So, $R \leqslant D_i \leqslant J$ by our induction hypothesis.
Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
Hence, $\Phi(S)_G$ is the Sylow $p$-subgroup of $J$.
Now, $R \leqslant \Phi(S)_G \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
Also, note that $R$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
(See, for example, Exercise 179 in \cite{rosetextbook}.)
By Lemma \ref{normal,containedinafrattini}, $R \leqslant \Phi(G)$.

Consider $G/R$.
Note that $J/R$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, and note also that $J/R \leqslant \Phi(G)R/R = \Phi(G/R)$.
Hence, $J/R$ is a Frattini normal subgroup of $G/R$.
The subgroup $S/R$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G/R$.
Since $[S/R, J/R] =[S,J]R/R \leqslant R/R$, we have that $J/R \leqslant \mathbf{Z}(S/R)$.
By Rose's Theorem (Theorem \ref{Rose'stheorem}), $J/R \leqslant \Phi(S/R)$.
As $R \leqslant \Phi(S)$, we have that $\Phi(S/R) = \Phi(S)/R$, and so $P \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
Now, since $P$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, we actually have that $P \leqslant \Phi(S)_G \leqslant J$.
Since $p$ was an arbitrary prime, this argument shows that each Sylow subgroup of $D_{i+1}$ is a subgroup of $J$.
Consequently, $D_{i+1} \leqslant J$.
The induction argument goes through.
In particular, $G' \cap \mathbf{Z}_{\infty}(G) \leqslant J$, as required.

label: F/Psiabelian
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{F/Psiabelian}
If $G$ is any group, then the section $\mathbf{F}(G)/\Psi(G)$ is abelian.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F = \mathbf{F}(G)$ and let $J = \Psi(G)$.
Let $p$ be a prime and let $P$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $F$.
Of course, as $F$ is nilpotent, we know that $P$ is a characteristic subgroup of $F$.
Since $F$ is normal in $G$, we deduce that $P$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
Now, since $P'$ is a characteristic subgroup of $P$ and $P$ is normal in $G$, the subgroup $P'$ is normal in $G$.

Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
Note that $P' \leqslant S$.
Because $P$ is nilpotent, $P' \leqslant \Phi(P)$.
Since $S$ is nilpotent, $\Phi(P) \leqslant \Phi(S)$ by Lemma \ref{nilpotentimpliesfrattinirespectscontainment}.
So, $P' \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
In fact, since $P'$ is normal in $G$, we have that $P' \leqslant \Phi(S)_G \leqslant J$.

Now, $PJ/J$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $F/J$.
Also, we have that $[PJ/J, PJ/J]=P'J/J = J/J$.
Hence, $PJ/J$ is abelian.
Since $p$ was arbitrary, the factor group $F/J$ has abelian Sylow subgroups.
The group $F/J$ is, therefore, nilpotent with abelian Sylow subgroups.
Hence, $F/J$ is abelian, and $F' \leqslant J$.
Indeed, the group $F/J$ is abelian.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md: If $G$ is any group, then the section $\mathbf{F}(G)/\Phi(G)$ is abelian.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $\mathbf{F}(G)' \leqslant \Psi(G)$ by Theorem \ref{F/Psiabelian}.
Hence $\mathbf{F}(G)' \leqslant \Phi(G)$, and so $\mathbf{F}(G)/\Phi(G)$ is abelian.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group and let $G = J\times R$ for subgroups $J$ and $R$ of $G$.
Then $\Psi(G) = \Psi(J) \times \Phi(R)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $p$ be a prime.
Let $J_p$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $J$ and let $R_p$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $R$.
Note that $S_p = J_p R_p = J_p \times R_p$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
By Lemma \ref{frattinisubgroupofdirectproduct}, $\Phi(S_p) = \Phi(J_p) \times \Phi(R_p)$.
Now, by Lemma \ref{coresofcertaintypesofsubgroupsindirectproducts}, $\Phi(S_p)_G = (\Phi(J_p) \Phi(R_p))_G = \Phi(J_p)_J\Phi(R_p)_R$.
Since $p$ was an arbitrary prime, we see 
\begin{align*}
\Psi(G) = \prod_{p \in \pi(G)} \Phi(S_p)_G &= \prod_{p\in \pi(G)} \Phi(J_p)_J \Phi(R_p)_R\\ &=\left(\prod_{p \in \pi(J)} \Phi(J_p)_J\right)\left(\prod_{p \in \pi(R)} \Phi(R_p)_R\right) \\
&= \Psi(J) \times \Psi(R),
\end{align*}
as wanted.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group and let $p$ be a prime.
Let $J$ be a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$ with $J \leqslant \Phi(G)$.
Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
If the commutator subgroup $[S,J]$ is normal in $G$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
So, in particular, $J \leqslant \Phi(S)_G \leqslant \Psi(G)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R = [S,J]$.
Then, by our hypothesis, $R$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.
Of course, $R \leqslant J$, as $J$ is normal in $G$ (and, therefore, $S$).
Consider the group $G/R$.
Note that $J/R$ is a normal $p$-subgroup of $G/R$ with $J/R \leqslant \Phi(G)R/R \leqslant \Phi(G/R)$.
Also, by a basic commutator identity, $[S/R, J/R]=[S,J]R/R= R/R$.
Hence, $J/R \leqslant \mathbf{Z}(S/R)$.
By Rose's Theorem applied in $G/R$, we deduce that $J/R \leqslant \Phi(S/R)$.
Note that $R \leqslant S'$.
Since $S$ is nilpotent, $S' \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
Hence, $\Phi(S/R) = \Phi(S)/R$ and $J\leqslant \Phi(S)$, as wanted.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group and let $p$ be a prime.
Let $J$ be a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$ with $J \leqslant \Phi(G)$.
Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
If $J \leqslant \mathbf{Z}_\infty(G)$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
So, in particular, $J \leqslant \Phi(S)_G \leqslant \Psi(G)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $H = \mathbf{Z}_\infty(G)$.
Let $R = [G, J]$, and note that $R$ is a normal subgroup of $\langle G, J \rangle = G$.
Now, $R \leqslant (G' \cap H) \leqslant \Psi(G)$ by Theorem \ref{G'intersecthypercenter}.
Since $R$ is a subgroup of $J$, we know that $R$ is a $p$-subgroup of $G$.
So, $R \leqslant (S \cap \Psi(G)) = \Phi(S)_G \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
Observe that $J/R$ is a normal subgroup of $G/R$ and that $J/R \leqslant \Phi(G)R/R \leqslant \Phi(G/R)$.
Also $[S/R, J/R] =[S,J]R/R = R/R$, and so $J/R \leqslant \mathbf{Z}(S/R)$.
By Rose's Theorem, $J/R \leqslant \Phi(S/R)$.
Now, since $R \leqslant \Phi(S)$, we know that $\Phi(S/R)  = \Phi(S)/R$.
Hence, $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$, as wanted.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $G$ be a group and let $p$ be a prime.
Let $J$ be a normal $p$-subgroup of $G$ with $J \leqslant \Phi(G)$.
Let $S$ be a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $J \leqslant \mathbf{Z}(S)$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If $J$ is cyclic, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If the subgroup $J \cap S'$ is normal in $G$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If the subgroup $[S,J]$ is normal in $G$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If $J \leqslant \mathbf{Z}_\infty(G)$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If $G$ is $p$-solvable of $p$-length $1$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If $G$ is $p$-solvable and each subgroup of $S$ can be generated by at most four elements and if $p =3$ and $\mathfrak{G}$ is not involved in $G$, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\item If $S$ is non-cyclic with $|S : \Phi(S)| = p^2$ and if either (a) $p = \min(\pi(G))$, (b) $S$ is generated by the elements of order $p$, or (c) $G$ is $p$-solvable, then $J \leqslant \Phi(S)$.
\end{enumerate}
